subjective.question: What is the single entry system of accounting? State its main features.
subjective.answer: Single entry system is a system of book keeping in which only personal accounts and a cash book are maintained, while real and nominal accounts are not recorded completely. It is therefore also called the system of incomplete records. Its main features are: (1) it is suitable for small businesses such as sole traders and small partnership firms; (2) a cash book mixing business and personal transactions is generally maintained; (3) original vouchers are the main source of information; (4) no trial balance can be prepared, so arithmetical accuracy cannot be checked; and (5) profit is ascertained by comparing the capital at the beginning and at the end of the period (net worth method).

subjective.question: Explain the net worth method of ascertaining profit under the single entry system.
subjective.answer: Under the net worth method, statements of affairs are prepared at the beginning and at the end of the accounting period. The excess of assets over liabilities in each statement gives the capital (net worth) at that date. The increase in capital during the year is then adjusted for the owner's personal transactions: drawings during the year are added back and fresh capital introduced is deducted. The resulting figure is the profit earned during the year (if negative, it is a loss). Formula: Profit = Closing Capital - Opening Capital + Drawings - Fresh Capital Introduced.

subjective.question: From the following information, calculate the profit of a trader for the year under the net worth method: Capital at the beginning of the year Rs. 150,000; Capital at the end of the year Rs. 190,000; Drawings during the year Rs. 25,000; Fresh capital introduced during the year Rs. 15,000.
subjective.answer: Increase in capital = Closing Capital - Opening Capital = 190,000 - 150,000 = Rs. 40,000. Adjustments: Add drawings (capital was reduced by personal withdrawals) = 40,000 + 25,000 = Rs. 65,000. Less fresh capital introduced (this increase is not profit) = 65,000 - 15,000 = Rs. 50,000. Profit for the year = Rs. 50,000.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a Statement of Affairs and a Balance Sheet.
subjective.answer: (1) Basis: A statement of affairs is prepared from incomplete records, while a balance sheet is prepared from complete double entry records. (2) Arithmetical accuracy: A statement of affairs is not based on a trial balance, so accuracy is not proved; a balance sheet agrees with the trial balance. (3) Capital: In a statement of affairs, capital is a balancing figure (assets minus liabilities); in a balance sheet, capital is taken from the capital account. (4) Omission: Assets or liabilities may be omitted unknowingly in a statement of affairs; omission is not possible in a balance sheet. (5) Purpose: A statement of affairs is prepared mainly to find opening/closing capital under single entry; a balance sheet shows the financial position under double entry.

subjective.question: How are credit sales and credit purchases ascertained under the single entry system?
subjective.answer: Credit sales are ascertained by preparing a Total Debtors Account: Opening balance of debtors + Credit sales (balancing figure) = Cash received from debtors + Discount allowed + Bad debts + Bills receivable received + Sales returns + Closing balance of debtors. The balancing figure of this account is the credit sales for the year. Similarly, credit purchases are ascertained by preparing a Total Creditors Account: Opening balance of creditors + Credit purchases (balancing figure) = Cash paid to creditors + Discount received + Bills payable accepted + Purchase returns + Closing balance of creditors. The balancing figure is the credit purchases for the year.

subjective.question: Differentiate between Receipts and Payments Account and Income and Expenditure Account.
subjective.answer: (1) Nature: Receipts and Payments Account is a real account (summary of the cash book); Income and Expenditure Account is a nominal account. (2) Basis: Receipts and Payments is on cash basis; Income and Expenditure is on accrual basis. (3) Period: Receipts and Payments records cash received/paid during the year whenever it arises (past, current or future period); Income and Expenditure records only income and expenses of the current year. (4) Items: Receipts and Payments includes both capital and revenue items; Income and Expenditure includes revenue items only. (5) Opening balance: Receipts and Payments starts with the opening cash/bank balance; Income and Expenditure has no opening balance. (6) Result: The closing balance of Receipts and Payments shows cash/bank in hand; the balance of Income and Expenditure shows surplus or deficit.

subjective.question: From the following information, calculate the amount of subscription to be credited to the Income and Expenditure Account for the year: Subscriptions received during the year Rs. 60,000; Outstanding subscriptions at the beginning of the year Rs. 4,000; Outstanding subscriptions at the end of the year Rs. 7,000; Subscriptions received in advance at the beginning of the year Rs. 2,000; Subscriptions received in advance at the end of the year Rs. 3,000.
subjective.answer: Subscription income = Amount received - Outstanding at the beginning (received this year but earned last year) + Outstanding at the end (earned this year, not yet received) + Advance at the beginning (received last year, earned this year) - Advance at the end (received this year, earned next year). = 60,000 - 4,000 + 7,000 + 2,000 - 3,000 = Rs. 62,000. Subscription income for the year = Rs. 62,000.

subjective.question: What is Capital Fund? How is it calculated in a non-trading concern?
subjective.answer: Capital Fund is the accumulated fund of a non-trading concern; it represents the excess of its assets over its liabilities and serves the same purpose as capital in a trading concern. It is calculated by preparing a Statement of Affairs (opening balance sheet) at the beginning of the year: Capital Fund = Total Assets - Total Liabilities. Example: if a club has assets of Rs. 500,000 and liabilities of Rs. 60,000 on the opening date, its Capital Fund is 500,000 - 60,000 = Rs. 440,000. Every year the surplus (or deficit) from the Income and Expenditure Account and capital receipts such as life membership fees and legacies are added to (or deducted from) this fund.

subjective.question: State the treatment of the following items in the accounts of a non-profit organization: (a) Entrance fee, (b) Life membership fee, (c) Legacy, (d) Donation for a specific purpose, (e) Sale of old fixed assets.
subjective.answer: (a) Entrance fee: Generally treated as a revenue receipt and credited to the Income and Expenditure Account, unless it is specifically required to be capitalized. (b) Life membership fee: A capital receipt, added to the Capital Fund in the Balance Sheet, because it is received once for the whole life of the member. (c) Legacy: Amount received under the will of a deceased person; it is a capital receipt and is added to the Capital Fund (unless the amount is small and recurring, when it may be treated as income). (d) Donation for a specific purpose: Shown as a liability/fund on the liabilities side of the Balance Sheet (e.g. Building Fund) and used only for that purpose; it is not credited to Income and Expenditure Account. (e) Sale of old fixed assets: The cash received is shown in the Receipts and Payments Account; in the Income and Expenditure Account only the profit or loss on sale (sale price minus book value) is shown, and the asset is removed from the Balance Sheet.

subjective.question: How is the amount of consumable items (e.g. stationery or sports materials) used during the year calculated for the Income and Expenditure Account?
subjective.answer: The amount consumed is calculated as: Opening stock of the item + Purchases during the year (cash purchases plus credit purchases, i.e. adjusted for outstanding amounts for purchases at the beginning and end of the year) - Closing stock of the item. Example: Opening stock of sports materials Rs. 8,000, purchases during the year Rs. 30,000 and closing stock Rs. 5,000; materials consumed = 8,000 + 30,000 - 5,000 = Rs. 33,000. This consumed amount is debited to the Income and Expenditure Account, while the closing stock appears as an asset in the Balance Sheet.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a dependent branch and an independent branch.
subjective.answer: (1) Books: A dependent branch does not maintain a complete set of books; the head office keeps all accounts. An independent branch maintains its own complete set of books under the double entry system. (2) Trial balance: A dependent branch does not prepare a trial balance; an independent branch prepares its own trial balance and final accounts. (3) Autonomy: A dependent branch works strictly under head office instructions and has no decision-making powers; an independent branch manager has powers regarding procurement, selling, pricing, advertising, staffing and even purchase of fixed assets. (4) Nature: A dependent branch is like a sales depot of the head office; an independent branch is treated as an investment centre. (5) Remittance: A dependent branch remits all cash received to the head office daily; an independent branch keeps its own bank account and meets its own expenses.

subjective.question: Explain the debtors system of branch accounting. How is branch profit ascertained under it?
subjective.answer: Under the debtors system, the head office opens a single Branch Account in its books for each branch, and all branch transactions are recorded in it. The Branch Account is debited with: opening balances of branch assets (stock, debtors, cash, petty cash, fixed assets), goods sent to branch (at cost, or at invoice price if sent so), and cash sent to branch for expenses. It is credited with: cash remitted by the branch to the head office, goods returned by the branch, and closing balances of branch assets. It is also debited with closing balances of branch liabilities and credited with opening balances of branch liabilities. The difference between the two sides of the Branch Account represents the profit (if credit side exceeds) or loss of the branch for the period.

subjective.question: Differentiate between the debtors system and the stock and debtor system of branch accounting.
subjective.answer: (1) Number of accounts: Under the debtors system only one Branch Account is maintained by the head office; under the stock and debtor system separate accounts are maintained - Branch Stock Account, Branch Debtors Account, Branch Cash Account, Branch Expenses Account, Goods Sent to Branch Account and Branch Adjustment Account. (2) Control: The debtors system provides no detailed control over branch stock; the stock and debtor system provides complete control over stock, debtors and cash of the branch. (3) Information: Gross profit and stock shortages cannot be located separately under the debtors system; under the stock and debtor system, gross profit is obtained from the Branch Adjustment Account and shortages/surpluses of stock are revealed by the Branch Stock Account. (4) Suitability: The debtors system is suitable for small branches; the stock and debtor system is suitable for large branches where goods are invoiced at selling/invoice price.

subjective.question: What are goods-in-transit and cash-in-transit? Give the journal entries passed for them at the end of the accounting year.
subjective.answer: Goods-in-transit are goods dispatched by the head office (or returned by the branch) before the year end but not received by the other party by that date. Cash-in-transit is the remittance sent by the branch which has not been received by the head office (or vice versa) before the closing date. Because the goods/cash have left one set of books but have not entered the other, an adjusting entry is passed by either the head office or the branch (not both) so that the two current accounts agree. Entries: (1) Goods-in-Transit Account Dr. - To Branch Account (in head office books) / To Head Office Account (in branch books). (2) Cash-in-Transit Account Dr. - To Branch Account (in head office books) / To Head Office Account (in branch books). At the start of the next year these entries are reversed.

subjective.question: What is 'loading' in branch accounting? Why does the head office invoice goods to the branch at a price higher than cost?
subjective.answer: Loading is the difference between the invoice price (the price at which goods are sent to the branch) and the cost price of the goods. The head office invoices goods at above cost for the following reasons: (1) to keep the cost price and the profit margin secret from the branch manager and staff; (2) to exercise effective control over branch stock, because stock can be checked at invoice price against sales and returns; (3) to avoid the need for the branch to calculate selling prices - the invoice price itself may be the selling price; and (4) to simplify branch stock records. Because accounts are kept at invoice price, the loading element in goods sent, returns and closing stock is adjusted through the Branch Adjustment Account / Stock Reserve Account so that profit is stated at cost-based figures.

subjective.question: A head office sends goods to its branch at invoice price, which is cost plus 25%. Goods sent to branch during the year were invoiced at Rs. 125,000 and the closing stock at the branch, at invoice price, is Rs. 25,000. Calculate (a) the loading on goods sent to branch and (b) the stock reserve to be created on closing stock.
subjective.answer: Invoice price = Cost + 25% of cost, so loading is 25/125 of the invoice price. (a) Loading on goods sent = 125,000 x 25/125 = Rs. 25,000. (b) Stock reserve on closing stock = 25,000 x 25/125 = Rs. 5,000. The stock reserve of Rs. 5,000 is created by debiting the Branch Adjustment Account (or Profit and Loss Account) and crediting the Stock Reserve Account, so that closing stock is shown in the Balance Sheet at its cost value of 25,000 - 5,000 = Rs. 20,000.

subjective.question: What are departmental accounts? Why are they maintained?
subjective.answer: Departmental accounts are accounts prepared separately for each department of a business so that the trading results of every department can be known individually. They are maintained for the following reasons: (1) to ascertain the profit or loss of each department separately; (2) to compare the performance of different departments and with previous periods; (3) to help management decide whether a department should be expanded, continued or closed; (4) to fix the remuneration/commission of departmental managers on the basis of departmental profit; and (5) to formulate policies for each department on the basis of its own results.

subjective.question: State the bases commonly used for apportioning the following common expenses among departments: (a) Rent and rates, (b) Lighting and heating, (c) Depreciation on building, (d) Selling and advertisement expenses, (e) Carriage inward, (f) Canteen and staff welfare expenses, (g) Insurance on stock, (h) Discount allowed.
subjective.answer: (a) Rent and rates: Floor area occupied by each department. (b) Lighting and heating: Number of light/heat points, or floor area occupied. (c) Depreciation on building: Floor area occupied by each department. (d) Selling and advertisement expenses: Sales (turnover) of each department. (e) Carriage inward: Purchases of each department. (f) Canteen and staff welfare expenses: Number of employees working in each department. (g) Insurance on stock: Value of stock held by each department. (h) Discount allowed: Sales of each department.

subjective.question: Total selling and distribution expenses of a business are Rs. 90,000. The sales of Departments A, B and C are Rs. 300,000, Rs. 200,000 and Rs. 100,000 respectively. Apportion the expenses among the departments.
subjective.answer: Selling and distribution expenses are apportioned on the basis of sales. Sales ratio = 300,000 : 200,000 : 100,000 = 3 : 2 : 1. Department A = 90,000 x 3/6 = Rs. 45,000. Department B = 90,000 x 2/6 = Rs. 30,000. Department C = 90,000 x 1/6 = Rs. 15,000. Total = 45,000 + 30,000 + 15,000 = Rs. 90,000.

subjective.question: Differentiate between fixed capital accounts and fluctuating capital accounts of partners.
subjective.answer: (1) Balance: Under the fixed capital method, the capital account balance remains unchanged except for fresh capital introduced or capital permanently withdrawn; under the fluctuating method, the balance changes with every adjustment. (2) Adjustments: Interest on capital, interest on drawings, salary, commission and share of profit/loss are recorded in a separate Current Account under the fixed method; under the fluctuating method all these are recorded in the Capital Account itself. (3) Number of accounts: Two accounts (Capital and Current) are maintained for each partner under the fixed method; only one account under the fluctuating method. (4) Debit balance: A current account may show a debit balance under the fixed method; under the fluctuating method the capital account itself may show a debit balance. (5) Agreement: The fixed method is used only when the partnership deed specifically provides for it; otherwise the fluctuating method is followed.

subjective.question: A and B are partners who share the profits in the ratio of 3/5 and 2/5 respectively. They admit C into partnership and the profit sharing ratio is agreed at 3/8 : 3/8 : 2/8 respectively. Calculate the sacrifice ratio of old partners.
subjective.answer: Sacrifice = Old ratio - New ratio. A's sacrifice = 3/5 - 3/8 = (24 - 15)/40 = 9/40. B's sacrifice = 2/5 - 3/8 = (16 - 15)/40 = 1/40. Sacrifice ratio of A and B = 9/40 : 1/40 = 9 : 1. The goodwill brought in by C will be shared by A and B in this sacrifice ratio of 9:1.

subjective.question: What is a Profit and Loss Appropriation Account? State the items appearing on its debit and credit sides.
subjective.answer: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account is an extension of the Profit and Loss Account, prepared by a partnership firm to show how the net profit of the business is distributed among the partners. Debit side: Interest on partners' capital, partners' salaries, partners' commission, amount transferred to general reserve, and the divisible profit transferred to partners' capital/current accounts in the profit sharing ratio. Credit side: Net profit brought down from the Profit and Loss Account, and interest on partners' drawings charged to the partners. Note: Interest on a partner's loan is not an appropriation; it is a charge against profits and is shown in the Profit and Loss Account.

subjective.question: The profits of a firm for the last three years were Rs. 40,000, Rs. 45,000 and Rs. 50,000. Goodwill is to be valued at 2 years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years. Calculate the value of goodwill.
subjective.answer: Total profits of three years = 40,000 + 45,000 + 50,000 = Rs. 135,000. Average profit = 135,000 / 3 = Rs. 45,000. Goodwill = Average profit x Number of years' purchase = 45,000 x 2 = Rs. 90,000.

subjective.question: What is a Revaluation Account? State the journal entries passed through it on the admission of a new partner.
subjective.answer: A Revaluation Account is a nominal account prepared at the time of admission, retirement or death of a partner (or change in profit sharing ratio) to record the increase or decrease in the value of assets and liabilities, so that the new partner does not share the profit or loss arising from values created before his admission. Entries on admission: (1) For increase in the value of an asset: Asset Account Dr. - To Revaluation Account. (2) For decrease in the value of an asset: Revaluation Account Dr. - To Asset Account. (3) For increase in a liability: Revaluation Account Dr. - To Liability Account. (4) For decrease in a liability: Liability Account Dr. - To Revaluation Account. (5) For an unrecorded liability: Revaluation Account Dr. - To Liability Account. The balance of the account (profit or loss on revaluation) is transferred to the old partners' capital accounts in their old profit sharing ratio.

subjective.question: State the rules applicable under the Partnership Act, 1932 in the absence of any agreement among the partners.
subjective.answer: In the absence of a partnership agreement (deed), the following rules of the Partnership Act, 1932 apply: (1) Profits and losses are shared equally by all partners, regardless of their capital contribution. (2) No interest is allowed on partners' capital. (3) No interest is charged on partners' drawings. (4) No salary or commission is payable to any partner for taking part in the business. (5) A partner who advances a loan to the firm beyond his capital is entitled to interest at 6% per annum on such loan. (6) Every partner has the right to take part in the conduct and management of the business, and the books of the firm are open to inspection by every partner.

subjective.question: How is the amount due to a retiring partner calculated and settled?
subjective.answer: On retirement, the amount due to the retiring partner is calculated by crediting his capital account with: his capital balance, his share of goodwill of the firm (valued and adjusted through the gaining partners), his share of profit on revaluation of assets and liabilities, his share of general reserve and accumulated profits, interest on capital and salary up to the date of retirement; and debiting it with: his drawings, interest on drawings, and his share of revaluation loss or accumulated losses. The net balance due is either paid immediately in cash or, if not paid, transferred to the Retiring Partner's Loan Account, which carries interest as agreed (6% per annum if there is no agreement) and is repaid in instalments or as agreed.

subjective.question: Differentiate between Profit and Loss Account and Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.
subjective.answer: (1) Stage: The Profit and Loss Account is prepared to ascertain the net profit of the business; the Appropriation Account is prepared after it, to show the distribution of that net profit. (2) Items: The Profit and Loss Account records all indirect expenses and incomes of the business, including charges such as interest on partners' loans and rent paid to a partner; the Appropriation Account records only appropriations of profit - interest on capital, partners' salaries and commission, interest on drawings and transfers to reserves. (3) Applicability: A Profit and Loss Account is prepared by every business; an Appropriation Account is prepared only by a partnership firm. (4) Starting point: The Profit and Loss Account starts with gross profit; the Appropriation Account starts with net profit brought down from the Profit and Loss Account.
